summary: Sirolimus is an mTOR-inhibitor immunosuppressant used to prevent organ rejection in renal transplant recipients aged 13 years and older. It carries a boxed warning for increased susceptibility to infection and development of lymphoma and other malignancies, and its use is NOT recommended in liver or lung transplant patients because of serious risks. Dosing is guided by whole-blood trough levels, and key adverse effects include hyperlipidemia, impaired wound healing, proteinuria, and interstitial lung disease.
indications: Prophylaxis of organ rejection in patients aged 13 years or older receiving renal (kidney) transplants

dosage.c: Renal transplant - low to moderate immunologic risk
dosage.d: Loading 6 mg, then 2 mg once daily; adjust to trough 16-24 ng/mL (with cyclosporine, first year)
dosage.n: Used with cyclosporine and corticosteroids; withdraw cyclosporine over 4-8 weeks at 2-4 months

dosage.d: Loading up to 15 mg, then 5 mg once daily; target trough 16-24 ng/mL
dosage.n: Continue with cyclosporine and corticosteroids for the first year

dosage.d: 2 mg once daily; adjust to trough 5-15 ng/mL
dosage.n: Reassess after 1-2 weeks of dose changes
Loading dose not changed; guide by trough levels

admin: Take once daily, consistently with or without food (the same way each day)
Take 4 hours after cyclosporine when the two are used together
Tablets must not be crushed, chewed, or split
For oral solution, dilute in water or orange juice (not grapefruit juice) and drink immediately
Avoid grapefruit juice, which inhibits sirolimus metabolism
moa: Sirolimus binds the intracellular protein FKBP-12 to form a complex that inhibits the mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR), a key regulatory kinase. This blocks the response of T and B lymphocytes to interleukin-2 and other cytokines, arresting the cell cycle at the G1-to-S transition and suppressing antigen- and cytokine-driven lymphocyte proliferation, thereby preventing graft rejection.

absolute: Use in liver transplant patients (increased mortality, graft loss, hepatic artery thrombosis) - not recommended
Use in lung transplant patients (bronchial anastomotic dehiscence, some fatal) - not recommended
relative: Significant proteinuria or declining renal function
Recent major surgery / open wounds (impaired healing)
monitor: Signs of infection, lung symptoms, and wound healing

preg: Sirolimus can cause fetal harm. Effective contraception is recommended before, during, and for 12 weeks after the final dose in females of reproductive potential. Avoid in pregnancy unless the benefit clearly outweighs the risk.
lact: Sirolimus is present in animal milk and excretion in human milk is likely; because of the potential for serious adverse reactions in the infant, breastfeeding is not recommended during treatment and for 12 weeks after the final dose.
renal: No initial dose adjustment for renal impairment, but sirolimus (especially with cyclosporine) can cause a decline in renal function and proteinuria. Monitor renal function and urinary protein closely and consider adjustment of the regimen.
hepatic: Reduce the maintenance dose in hepatic impairment (approximately one-third for mild-moderate and about one-half for severe impairment); the loading dose need not be modified. Guide adjustments by whole-blood trough concentrations.

major: Strong CYP3A4/P-gp inhibitors (ketoconazole, itraconazole, voriconazole, clarithromycin, erythromycin, ritonavir) - markedly increase sirolimus levels; avoid
Strong CYP3A4/P-gp inducers (rifampin, rifabutin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital) - decrease levels and efficacy; avoid
Cyclosporine (increases sirolimus exposure; separate dosing by 4 hours and monitor renal function)
minor: Drugs that prolong wound healing or affect lipids
interactions.food: Grapefruit juice inhibits CYP3A4 and raises sirolimus levels - avoid; take consistently relative to food
interactions.alcohol: No direct interaction; limit alcohol given hepatic/metabolic considerations
interactions.diagnostics: Can raise serum cholesterol and triglycerides, alter LFTs, and lower blood counts

serious: Increased risk of serious infections (including opportunistic and reactivation of latent virus)
Impaired or delayed wound healing and fluid accumulation
Proteinuria and decline in renal function
Hemolytic uremic syndrome / thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura / thrombotic microangiopathy
emergency: Acute interstitial pneumonitis with respiratory failure

monitoring: Whole-blood sirolimus trough concentrations (especially after dose or interacting-drug changes)
Signs of infection and pulmonary symptoms
counsel: Take it exactly as prescribed, always the same way with respect to food, and 4 hours after cyclosporine if you take both
It weakens the immune system - report fevers, cough, breathlessness, or other signs of infection promptly
Use effective contraception and avoid pregnancy and breastfeeding during and for 12 weeks after treatment
Protect your skin from the sun and report any new skin lesions
Do not stop or change the dose, and keep all blood-test appointments
pk: Immunosuppressive effect develops over days as steady state is reached
Peak whole-blood concentration about 1-3 hours after oral dosing
Long terminal half-life, approximately 62 hours (range ~46-78 h)
Tablets and solution: store at 20-25 C, protect from light; refrigerate solution (2-8 C) per labeling
pearls: BOXED WARNING: increased susceptibility to infection and to lymphoma/other malignancies from immunosuppression
NOT recommended in liver transplant (hepatic artery thrombosis, graft loss, death) or lung transplant (bronchial dehiscence) patients
Dose by whole-blood trough levels; long half-life means changes take days to reach steady state
Watch for hyperlipidemia, proteinuria, poor wound healing, and pneumonitis; separate from cyclosporine by 4 hours
missed: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember unless it is close to the next dose. Do not take a double dose. Tell your transplant team about missed doses, as consistent levels are important.
overdose: Reports of acute overdose are limited; expected effects relate to exaggerated immunosuppression and adverse reactions. There is no specific antidote. Management is supportive; sirolimus is highly bound and not appreciably dialyzable, so general supportive measures and monitoring of blood levels and organ function are used.
